newsitem.title: GERMANY: Truckers' strikes disrupt commerce across Europe.
newsitem.headline: Truckers' strikes disrupt commerce across Europe.

text.p: Truckers' strikes in France and Denmark sent waves of agitation throughout Europe on Wednesday, clogging highways and ports and disrupting commerce.
French truckers blockaded highways along the borders on the 10th day of their strike, inconveniencing merchants, consumers and drivers in neighbouring countries.

The strikes threatened to disrupt production at Volkswagen AG, Europe's largest carmaker, and hampered delivery of fresh fruit, vegetables, fish, spirits and gourmet foods from France, Scandinavia, Spain and elsewhere.

Thousands of drivers from Germany and other countries were ensnared by the blockades without enough food or money and growing tension led to sometimes violent confrontations with French truckers, the German Transport Association said.
"The French strike leaders apparently want to increase the pressure on the French government and employers by laming cross-border traffic," the association said.
German Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann appealed to his counterparts in France and Denmark to help German drivers stranded there and limit the damage to German companies.
Lorries forced by the French strike to detour through the Belgian port of Zeebrugge faced big tailbacks and 20-hour waiting times to board ferries.
"It is totally blocked. There are more than 1,000 trucks and more coming," a spokesman for the port police said. "They can't get through Calais so they are all coming here on the way to Dover."

But Stena-Sally Lines ferries from Ostend to Ramsgate were reporting booming business as trucks were rerouted from the Calais-Dover crossing. "All our sailings are fully booked with freight lorries," a spokesman said. "Normally at this time of year they are only half full."

A spokesman for the Belgian Transport Association said the French strike was costing Belgian haulage firms millions of francs. "It is impossible to get to Spain by road at all, and getting to Italy you have to detour through Luxembourg, Germany and Switzerland which has a 28-tonne weight limit."
While most German merchants reported prices of fish and produce were still steady, supplies were running short. They feared sales would drop if the strike went on.

"We got no delivery (from France) today," said chef Thomas Daehner at the restaurant La Marmite in Bonn. "The truck was stopped at the border. The poor driver can't get through and the goods are spoiling."
La Marmite buys fish, mussels and poultry from France and will now have to find alternative supplies in Germany, he said.
VW union officials said the car maker may have to cut back production at its plants in Wolfsburg and Brussels for lack of key parts that arrive from France. A decision is due on Monday.
Employers in France agreed on Wednesday to one of the striking truckers' key demands, allowing them to retire early, but the strike went on over higher pay and shorter hours.
A stoppage by French pilots and air crews cut flights on Wednesday, worsening travellers' woes.
The Danish truckers' strike, unrelated to the one in France, has left almost a million export-bound Christmas trees rotting at the border, dealing a serious blow to the industry.

Denmark is the world's largest exporter of Christmas trees, and Germany buys over 60 percent of its shipments. The Danish truckers are protesting against government plans to cut drivers' overseas subsistence allowances.
On Wednesday, they appeared divided over whether to blockade Copenhagen.
